short: Valerian's edicts targeted Christian clergy and property before his capture ended the campaign.
full:
In 257 the emperor Valerian issued an edict exiling Christian bishops, priests and deacons and banning Christian assembly and access to cemeteries. A harsher edict followed in 258, ordering the execution of clergy, the death or forced labour of Christian senators and knights who refused to recant, and confiscation of the property of Christians in the imperial household. Bishop Cyprian of Carthage and Pope Sixtus II were among those executed under its terms.

The persecution ended abruptly when Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I in 260, an unprecedented humiliation that left him a prisoner until his death. His son and co-emperor Gallienus reversed the policy soon after, issuing an edict of toleration that restored confiscated property and granted Christians the first legal recognition of their right to assemble, a peace that held for four decades.
